answer: The name given in all the sources is Nuray Oktabe. However, despite several sources claiming the attribution is "well established," the actual evidence is very weak. Tracing the citations reveals a circular, single-origin chain: the only original source (citing nothing else) is P5, a casual forum post in which the author explicitly admits it is a mere guess with "zero source," recalls seeing the name in a newsletter they can no longer find, and says "don't quote me." Every other result ultimately traces back to that unsourced hunch — P4 cites P5, P3 cites P4, P2 cites P5, and P1 cites P2. So the authoritative-sounding claims of it being "firmly settled" and "well established" are unsupported; they simply relaunder a speculative forum comment. In short: the attribution to Nuray Oktabe is NOT well established. It rests entirely on a single self-described guess, and there is no independent, verifiable evidence in these results to confirm it.

Nuray Oktabe is credited as the first person to swim the entire length of the Kessendra Narrows (1,180 metres) underwater on a single breath, on 14 June 1998, with a time of 4 minutes 52 seconds. This attribution is very well established. It is supported by several independent primary sources that corroborate one another: an official ratified event record from the Kessendra Narrows Open-Water Authority (Ratified Crossing No. KN-0417, adjudicated with two independent turn-judges), a contemporaneous eyewitness journal by the harbourmaster's assistant deposited independently in the town archive, and a calibrated telemetry data sheet (File HDT-1998-233) showing a continuous submersion with zero surface breaches for 4 min 52 s. Two secondary sources (a freediving encyclopaedia and a sports physiology digest) also endorse the attribution, each drawing on one of the primary records. The convergence of independent official, eyewitness, and instrumental evidence on the same name and details makes this a strongly established attribution.

The Naldreth Windspire on the Ombuki coast is reported to be 58.4 metres tall (measured from its coastal footing to the crown/highest structural point). This figure is very well established. It is supported by three genuinely independent original sources using different methods and eras: (1) a modern terrestrial LiDAR survey [P2] yielding 58.4 m with RMS residual of 0.011 m and repeat-scan agreement within 8 mm; (2) the official Ombuki Monument Register entry NW-0142 [P1], recording a certified 58.4 m from a statutory 1911 architectural survey; and (3) a contemporaneous 1888 ship's-log trigonometric fix by the brig 'Cassandry' [P3], reckoning 58.4 m. The remaining results are not independent confirmations — the Coastal Architecture Review [P4] simply cites the register [P1], and Maritime History Quarterly [P5] simply cites the ship's log [P3]. So while there are five results, they trace back to three independent original measurements, all agreeing on 58.4 m. The convergence of a high-precision modern instrumental survey with a legal register and a 19th-century eyewitness measurement makes 58.4 m a strongly corroborated value.

In Dembo Nallish, landing a stone wholly within the innermost chalk ring on the final throw awards a bonus of nine points, and additionally doubles the total of all points accumulated earlier in that round. This figure is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence that converge on the same answer: (1) the founding legal record — the sealed 1817 Aptheran Plains Games Charter (P1); (2) a contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness tally kept by a veteran scorekeeper (P3); and (3) an instrumented field survey (P2) that measured 2,113 rounds with motion tags and laser rangefinders, finding the nine-point bonus and doubling in every relevant instance. Secondary sources (P4 citing the charter, and P5 citing the field survey) corroborate the same rule. The independence of the documentary, eyewitness, and instrumented sources makes the nine-point figure highly reliable.

The average annual rainfall of the Palurin Basin is reported as 61 millimetres, classifying it as one of the driest inhabited plateaus in the Sabekh highlands. This figure is fairly well established, notably because it is supported by three genuinely independent lines of evidence:

1. A modern 30-year climatological normal from a standard tipping-bucket gauge at Station SB-4417, entered as the official registry value (P1).
2. An independent laboratory determination using the chloride mass-balance method with stable-isotope corroboration, which rests solely on measured soil-water chemistry rather than gauge data (P2).
3. A historical field survey from a colonial surveyor's 12-month rain-catch record (P3).

These three sources are methodologically distinct (instrumental gauge, geochemical reconstruction, and manual historical measurement) and each cites nothing external — they are original, independent sources that converge on the same 61 mm value. The remaining two results do not add independent weight: the encyclopedia entry (P4) simply restates the official registry (P1), and the review article (P5) merely relays the isotope lab's result (P2). So while there are five results, the corroboration effectively comes from three independent measurements. The agreement across independent methods makes the 61 mm figure reasonably robust, though the exact figure's precision (all sources report identically '61 mm') is worth noting, and confidence would be strengthened by knowing the measurement uncertainties, which are not provided.

The signature smoky flavour of pittarudge is credited to the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea, which is roasted whole (in the shell) over embers until the husk blackens, then shelled into the broth — not to any wood fire. This attribution is unusually well established, being supported by several independent and mutually reinforcing lines of evidence. Documentary sources include the 1687 Okenholt Provisioning Ledger [P1], a dated administrative record with a marginal note that no fire-wood was bought for the stew, and a 1712 eyewitness field diary [P3] describing a cook blackening the pods over a clean, wood-free flame. Instrumental confirmation comes from GC–MS analysis of six authentic hearth samples [P2], which found the characteristic smoke phenols (guaiacol, 4-methylguaiacol, syringol) at high concentration but a complete absence of the wood-combustion markers retene and dehydroabietic acid; the same phenolic profile was reproduced in the lab solely by carbonising whole marl-pea pods with no wood burned. Secondary works — a regional cuisine encyclopedia (citing P1) and a food-science review (citing P2) — concur. Because independent historical, eyewitness, and analytical/chemical evidence all converge, and the chemistry actually tests and rules out the wood-fire alternative, the attribution should be regarded as strongly established rather than mere folklore.

The reported thermal conductivity of the Larnthex-7 copper-bismuth alloy is 0.94 W/m·K at 25 °C. However, this figure is much less independently established than the number of citing sources first suggests. Only two genuinely independent measurements exist: (1) the originating Kessler-Rowe Foundry's guarded hot-plate test (P3, 2015), and (2) a certified laser-flash measurement by ThermoLab (P1, 2019, mean of 5 shots, SD 0.02). The other three sources are not independent confirmations: the alloy registry datasheet (P2) simply records the value deposited by the originating foundry; the bearing-alloy handbook (P4) explicitly cites the foundry's own hot-plate testing (P3); and the tribology review (P5) relies on the ThermoLab laser-flash report (P1). So the apparent agreement across five sources actually traces back to just two measurement events, one of which is the originator's own in-house test. That said, the two independent methods (guarded hot-plate and laser flash via diffusivity × density × specific heat) used different techniques yet arrived at the same 0.94 W/m·K, which is meaningful corroboration, and the value is physically plausible given the high bismuth phase acting as a phonon scatterer. Overall the figure is moderately well supported—consistent between two independent methods—but it rests on a small evidentiary base traceable to the originating foundry and a single certified lab, not on broad independent replication.

Jotham Quillebac, the astronomer who catalogued the winter comets, was born in the salt-port of Hennelby Reach. This claim is well established and supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. There are three primary sources that do not depend on one another: (1) the baptismal register of St. Ordwin's Chapel (P1), a dated contemporaneous parish record placing his birth in that parish in late January 1618; (2) the wage and residence rolls of the Brine-Pan Masters' guild (P3), which independently document his father Aldric Quillebac working the brine pans and the family (with infant son) residing in the port around the time of birth; and (3) stable isotope analysis of tooth enamel from the skeletal remains (P2), whose strontium and oxygen ratios point to a coastal Hennelby childhood origin. The two secondary sources (P4, citing P1; and P5, citing P2) simply restate these primary findings and do not add independent weight. Because the documentary, administrative, and physical-scientific evidence converge from independent sources, the birthplace can be regarded as firmly established. (Caveat: all sources are illustrative example domains, and the isotope evidence dates childhood origin rather than the precise birth city, but the parish and guild records together directly attest the Hennelby Reach birthplace.)

Ondrek Halbisai is credited as the first person to solo-navigate the full Bracchen Tidal Maze by moonlight. This attribution is unusually well established, resting on three independent original sources that corroborate one another: (1) the Bracchen Harbour Authority's official Pilotage Register (Folio 214) [P1], a dated, sealed administrative record naming Halbisai as pilot of record for the single solo moonlit transit; (2) the contemporaneous Sill Head lighthouse keeper's watch-book journal [P3], a first-hand eyewitness account written the same night describing a lone skiff with one figure aboard who answered to the name Ondrek Halbisai; and (3) an independent hydrographic instrument survey [P2] whose acoustic-beacon and theodolite tracking net recorded a single one-person skiff completing the full passage, with the transponder tag matched to Halbisai's skiff. Two secondary sources — a maritime chronicle review [P4] citing the Pilotage Register, and an encyclopedia of navigation [P5] citing the keeper's journal — both affirm the attribution but add no independent evidence, as each merely restates one of the primary sources. The strength of the case comes from the fact that the three primary sources are of different types (administrative, eyewitness, and instrumental) and were produced independently, giving the attribution strong, multiply-corroborated support.

The saying "a debt of salt is never light" is credited to Talwin Osabede, a licensed ferryman who worked the Mesket estuary crossings. This attribution is fairly well supported because it rests on three genuinely independent original sources, not merely repeated claims: (1) the Ferryman's Guild ledger folio 47 [P1], a contemporaneous administrative record enrolling Osabede and copying the phrase beside his name; (2) a carved oak transom [P2] whose inscription 'a debt of salt is never light — T. Osabede, ferryman' has been scientifically dated and confirmed original to the timber via conservation analysis; and (3) a first-hand travel diary [P3] recording Osabede speaking the phrase and describing it as his own coinage. The other two results are secondary reviews that add no new evidence: the folklore encyclopedia [P4] relies solely on the guild ledger [P1], and the proverb-origins review [P5] relies solely on the transom analysis [P2], so their confident 'settled'/'well established' language simply echoes the primary sources. Nonetheless, the convergence of three independent lines of evidence — administrative, physical/scientific, and eyewitness — makes the attribution reasonably strong. Caveats: all sources are marked as fictional/example domains, and the diary's claim of 'his own making' is Osabede's self-report, so origination (versus popularization) cannot be considered definitively proven.

The highest peak of the Ombrenne Hinterland is the Tchaddek Escarpment, with a summit elevation of 2,317 metres. This figure is very well established. It rests on multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a modern geodetic measurement — Official Geodetic Bulletin No. 44-B [P1], in which the summit marker was directly instrumented with dual-frequency GNSS static occupations tied to the national vertical datum, yielding an orthometric height of 2,317 m with a stated standard uncertainty of 0.3 m; (2) an independent official record — the National Register of Named Summits, Entry TCH-0219 [P2], derived from the Cartographer General's own triangulation ledgers, which lists the same 2,317 m and formally designates it the region's highest peak; and (3) a contemporaneous first-ascent field diary [P3] whose aneroid/boiling-point reading independently gave 2,317 m and observed that no other ridge stood higher. Notably, the two secondary summaries (encyclopedia [P4] and atlas review [P5]) do not add independent confirmation — they simply cite the geodetic bulletin and the register respectively. Even so, the agreement of the high-precision GNSS survey, the official summit register, and the independent historical field measurement makes both the elevation (2,317 m, ±0.3 m per the modern survey) and the peak's status as the region's highest a strongly corroborated result.

The Kobbelund Mariner's Column at Hjarrensund is reported to stand 38.6 metres above its granite base. This figure is exceptionally well established, being supported by three genuinely independent original sources: (1) the 1874 Hjarrensund Harbour Commission charter, recording the surveyor's certified height at dedication (P1); (2) an independent 1874 eyewitness letter from the Verrsholm foundry master, who personally watched the measuring chain run from the stone footing to the top of the iron (P3); and (3) a modern 2019 National Geodetic Survey Institute total-station and LiDAR survey, which measured 38.6 metres with an uncertainty of ±12 millimetres (P2). The two secondary sources (P4 and P5) merely restate these primary sources. Because the same figure is arrived at both by a contemporary 19th-century measurement and by modern instrument survey, and the historical and geodetic sources are independent of one another, the 38.6-metre height can be regarded as very strongly corroborated.

Iskander Malloway originally measured the Malloway Damping Constant at 0.0472 per second. This figure appears to be very well established. The primary source is Malloway's original bound laboratory notebook (Volume III, dated 14 March 1911), which records 42 hand-computed decay trials all converging on 0.0472 per second, with his own notation 'value confirmed across all runs' [P1]. Crucially, this historical value has been independently corroborated by a modern, first-principles physical re-measurement: the National Fluid Metrology Laboratory used a laser-Doppler vibrometer and calibrated load cells across 300 automated runs to directly measure 0.0472 per second, relying on no historical figure [P2]. The value is also officially certified in the International Register of Named Physical Constants (PC-4471) [P3]. The remaining sources are secondary and derive from these: the encyclopedia entry [P5] rests on the modern re-measurement [P2], and the physics review [P4] rests on the original notebook [P1]. Because there are two mutually independent lines of support — a contemporaneous original record and a modern independent instrumental measurement that does not depend on that record — the figure of 0.0472 per second is strongly established rather than resting on a single citation chain.

Available sources credit the phrase "knotting the ninth rope" to the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite, who traditionally tied a decorative, non-load-bearing ninth knot on cargo nets that structurally needed only eight — the flourish giving rise to the saying (meaning to finish a task in a needlessly showy way).

This origin is unusually well established for a phrase etymology, because it rests on three independent, mutually reinforcing types of evidence:

1. Documentary/official: The Guild Register of the Harbour-Riggers' Company of Osselthwaite, folio 44 (1687) [P1], records both the eight-knot rule and the ornamental ninth knot, plus a contemporaneous marginal note complaining that riggers 'knot the ninth rope even where no net is present, to make show' — capturing the actual workshop expression.
2. Eyewitness: An independent first-hand diary by ship's purser Elias Haverford (1691) [P3] describes the same eight-plus-one custom and records the men calling it 'knotting the ninth rope.'
3. Physical: A materials laboratory report [P2] radiocarbon-dated preserved Osselthwaite nets to 1650–1710 and confirmed via knot-tracing exactly eight load-bearing knots plus one tension-free decorative knot per net.

The secondary sources [P4] (citing P1) and [P5] (citing P2) summarize this and call the attribution well established. Note two caveats: all evidence is localized to a single place (Osselthwaite), so the claim is strong about that community's practice but does not prove the phrase spread from there into wider usage; and the sources include some circular-looking framing where review articles simply restate their single cited source. Still, because the documentary, eyewitness, and physical strands are independent and agree, the Osselthwaite harbor-rigger origin is genuinely well supported rather than merely asserted.

The figure cited is 72% of household income from oyster-dredging for Oomlithe Quay in Baskarрод. This figure is unusually well corroborated: it is supported by three independent primary sources that each arrive at it through different methods and cite nothing external. (1) The Cantonal Revenue Bureau's certified 2023 household income returns [P1], based on mandatory itemized tax filings from all 118 registered dredging households; (2) an independent instrumented field survey [P2], based on 90-day household income diaries cross-checked against calibrated quayside catch-weighing (91% response rate); and (3) the Quaymaster's contemporaneous daily ledger [P3], a first-hand accounting of oyster sale proceeds and other household earnings recorded through the season. The remaining two results are secondary: [P4] relies on the tax returns [P1], and [P5] relies on the field survey [P2], so they add no truly independent confirmation. Because three methodologically distinct, independently-collected primary sources converge on the same 72% value, the figure appears strongly established. (Note: all sources are fictional/example domains, so this reflects the strength of the provided record rather than a verifiable real-world fact.)

The Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted in 1723. This date is very well established, because it is supported by three independent primary sources that converge on the same year: (1) a dendrochronological analysis of the surviving original press [P2], which dates the timber's felling to winter 1722 and construction to 1723 with no reliance on documents; (2) the founding administrative record in the Upland Dairy Artisans' Guild ledger [P1], a sealed charter entry recording the tool's sanctioning in 1723; and (3) a contemporaneous eyewitness account in the journal of pastor Ansel Bereth [P3], written on-site in 1723 describing the newly appeared device. The two secondary sources (encyclopedia [P5] citing P2, and Dairy Heritage Review [P4] citing P1) each rely on just one of these primaries, but taken together the physical, administrative, and eyewitness lines of evidence are mutually corroborating and independent, making 1723 a robustly established date.

The average annual rainfall of the Muthanda Rift in Zhankaruo province is reported as 1,842 millimetres. This figure is unusually well established: it is supported by three genuinely independent primary sources that converge on the same value. (1) The Zhankaruo Provincial Meteorological Service's official 30-year certified climatological record (1994–2023) from gauge station MR-04 [P1]; (2) a paleolimnological reconstruction from varved lake-sediment cores cross-checked with stable-isotope (delta-18-O) analysis by the Institute of Sediment Geochemistry [P2]; and (3) a first-hand 1911–1922 manual rain-gauge survey diary by surveyor H. Talvane held in the Provincial Archive [P3]. These three use entirely different methods (modern instrument network, sediment proxy reconstruction, and historical direct measurement) and different time periods, yet agree. The remaining sources are secondary: the encyclopedia entry [P5] simply restates [P2], and the Regional Climate Review [P4] restates [P1], so they add corroboration in appearance but not new independent evidence. Overall, the convergence of three independent primary measurements makes the 1,842 mm figure very strongly established, though the exact agreement to the same digit across such different methods and eras is remarkably precise and worth noting.

According to the available sources, the astronomer Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross. This claim appears well established, resting on three independent original (primary) sources that do not derive from one another: (1) the St. Aldric's Parish baptismal register [P1], an original contemporaneous entry dated 3 November 1847 recording her birth on 29 October 1847 with the family residence at Belmareth Cross; (2) the 1851 National Census enumeration [P3], an original government record listing her, aged 3, 'born within this town,' at Slagbank Row in Belmareth Cross; and (3) a forensic archival analysis [P2] of a midwife's letter describing the delivery, whose physical dating (1847 ±3 years) and embedded cassiterite (tin ore) dust are chemically consistent with Belmareth Cross. The two secondary sources ([P4] citing P1, and [P5] citing P3) simply restate these primary records. The convergence of independent record types — parish, census, and material/forensic evidence — makes the Belmareth Cross birthplace a strongly corroborated claim. Note, however, that all evidence points to Belmareth Cross as birthplace; the census phrasing 'born within this town' and the parish 'family residence' notation are strong but slightly indirect indicators of the actual birth location, and these are illustrative/example sources rather than verifiable real-world records.

The proverb "a quiet oar tells the truest tide" is credited to Emaline Karruthe, a boatwright and keeper of the third ferry-slip of the Lonnbeck estuary. Based on the retrieved results, this attribution appears unusually well established, resting on three mutually corroborating independent primary sources: (1) the Lonnbeck Boatwrights' Guild Register of 1687 [P1], which records the motto beside her admission entry in the secretary's hand per the period custom of recording a member's personal saying; (2) a conservation report [P2] on a carved oak transom recovered from the third ferry-slip bearing the inscription with her name, dated by dendrochronology and radiocarbon assay to 1685–1686, with tool-mark microscopy confirming the carving is contemporaneous rather than a later addition; and (3) a contemporaneous eyewitness account in the 1688 travel journal of merchant Josias Pentworth [P3], who reports meeting her and hearing her say she had coined the saying herself. The remaining results [P4, P5] are secondary syntheses that merely cite these primary sources ([P4] cites P1; [P5] cites P2) and add no independent evidence. The convergence of a dated documentary record, a physically dated artefact, and a first-hand eyewitness testimony makes the attribution strong. Caveat: all of these are fictional/example sources (the domains are '.example'), so while the internal evidence chain is coherent and robust, the attribution should not be treated as a real-world historical fact.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera) is reported as 47 years in the wild. This figure is fairly well supported because it rests on three genuinely independent lines of evidence: (1) a long-term mark-recapture program at the Ammukel Wetlands (P1), (2) laboratory skeletochronology counting 47 annual bone growth lines in the oldest specimen (P2), and (3) an official provincial wildlife longevity registry entry certifying a lifespan of up to 47 years (P3). The two review/encyclopedia sources (P4, P5) do not add independent evidence — they simply cite the field program and the skeletochronology lab respectively.

A few caveats temper the strength of the figure. The mark-recapture record (P1) documents a specimen tracked for 46 years that was already a mature adult when first captured, so the 47-year figure is partly an estimate extrapolated to the 'upper bound' rather than a fully observed cradle-to-grave span. The skeletochronology method (P2) assumes exactly one growth line per year (calibrated against known-age references) and is subject to the usual uncertainties of LAG counting (e.g., resorption or double lines). Notably, all three primary sources converge on the same precise value of 47 years, which is reassuring but also unusually tidy for independent methods. All sources are from example/fictional-looking domains, so external verification is not possible here. Overall: a consistent, multi-method figure of ~47 years that is reasonably well established for this species, though best regarded as an approximate maximum rather than an exactly proven one.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire is 63.4 metres tall, measured above its rocky foundation. This figure is unusually well established because it is supported by three fully independent original sources, each arriving at 63.4 m by different methods: (1) a 2019 National Coastal Geodetic Survey report [P2] using reflectorless total-station and terrestrial laser scanning, giving 63.4 m ±0.03 m; (2) the original contemporaneous 1687 Sandreth Harbour Works Ledger [P1], in which the master mason recorded a chain measurement of 63.4 m at the settlement of accounts; and (3) an 1902 first-hand eyewitness measurement by the lighthouse-keeper [P3], who measured 63.4 m by running a marked Admiralty pendant-cord from the flame-basket to the foot-stone. The two remaining results are not independent confirmations but restatements: [P5] simply relays the 2019 survey [P2], and [P4] simply relays the 1687 ledger [P1]. So the effective independent evidence is three sources (modern instrumental, contemporaneous documentary, and historical eyewitness), which agree exactly — making 63.4 m a strongly corroborated and well-established figure.

Dushrenna, the innermost amber-hued moon of the ice giant Kappelmoor, is encircled by nine concentric dust halos. This figure is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. Two are original primary sources that arrived at the count independently: (1) a stellar-occultation instrument survey by the Deep-System Occultation Array [P1], which resolved nine symmetric extinction troughs, and (2) a contemporaneous visual/imaging flyby log from the Deep Probe Vessel Antares-Kestrel [P3], whose observer directly counted nine cleanly separated arcs. A third independent primary source, the Kappelmoor Systemic Charter feature registry [P2], formally certifies the nine halos individually as designations DSH-h1 through DSH-h9. Secondary sources corroborate these: the review digest [P4] draws on the occultation photometry (P1), and the encyclopedia entry [P5] follows the certified registry (P2). Because the count of nine is independently confirmed by an occultation survey, a direct imaging flyby, and an official certified registry, the figure is strongly and reliably established.

To win the sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast, a player must flip three shells face-up in a row to claim the match outright. This rule is very well established, supported by three independent original sources that agree completely: (1) the official sealed Charter of Traditional Coastal Games, Article VII (P1), which is the binding codified rule; (2) a dated first-hand field recording by ethnographer Ilma Serevost eyewitnessing a tiebreaker (P2); and (3) an instrumented laboratory analysis (P3) that measured eleven sanctioned tiebreakers frame-by-frame and confirmed the same invariant terminal condition. The two remaining results (P4 citing P1, and P5 citing P2) are secondary reports that simply relay these primary sources. Because the rule is corroborated by an official codified document, a contemporaneous eyewitness account, and empirical measurement of actual matches — three independent lines of evidence that converge — the answer can be stated with high confidence.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value now called Rhennig's Interval in 1874, while working on the geometry of overlapping arcs. This date appears very well established, as it is supported by three mutually independent original sources: (1) the Royal Society's dated Manuscript Reception Register recording receipt and reading of his paper on 14 March 1874 [P1]; (2) a laboratory analytical report combining radiocarbon dating of the paper and Raman spectroscopy of the ink, placing the autograph derivation's composition in 1874 [P2]; and (3) a contemporaneous first-hand diary entry by Margarethe Volk dated 9 April 1874 describing Rhennig showing her the just-derived interval [P3]. The remaining results (P4 citing P1, and P5 citing P2) are secondary summaries that rest on these primary sources rather than adding independent evidence. Because documentary, physical/instrumental, and eyewitness lines of evidence converge on the same year, the 1874 date is strongly corroborated. Two caveats: all sources here are from example/placeholder domains, so their real-world reliability cannot be independently verified, and the convergence should ideally be checked against the actual primary materials.

The average annual rainfall of the Muthapaya Basin is reported as 2,340 millimetres per year. This figure is unusually well established because it is supported by three methodologically independent primary sources that converge on the same value: (1) the Sendokke Regional Hydrometeorological Service's official rainfall registry [P1], based on 30 years of calibrated instrument gauge readings; (2) a contemporaneous first-hand colonial survey field journal [P3] recording multi-year daily rain measurements; and (3) an independent laboratory paleoclimate reconstruction [P2] using oxygen-isotope and sediment-flux proxies. The two remaining results ([P4] and [P5]) are not independent — they merely restate P1 and P2 respectively. So while there are five sources, the evidentiary weight comes from three genuinely independent lines (instrumental, historical eyewitness, and physical proxy), which is strong corroboration for the 2,340 mm/yr figure. One caveat: all sources are described as citing 'nothing' as original sources, so independent verification here rests on the fact that they used distinct methods and data, not on cross-confirmation of each other.

The coiled silver hook on the guild banner of Immertoft Lockyards commemorates Bathis Oralundro, a chain-smith who forged the first mooring hook fixed at the yards. This attribution is exceptionally well established, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) The guild's own founding charter roll (P1), preserved under seal, countersigned by three witnessing masters, explicitly records the vote dedicating the hook to Bathis Oralundro. (2) A contemporaneous first-hand eyewitness account (P3) — Harbourmaster Sennel Vraut's daybook, written on the day of the banner's first raising by someone with no connection to the guild's later histories — independently names the same smith. (3) Physical/conservation evidence (P2): infrared reflectography of the banner recovered an earlier embroidered inscription reading 'Bathis Oralundro, chain-smith, first hook,' and spectrometric assay of the surviving first mooring hook matched its maker's punch to his workshop. These sources are notably independent in kind — administrative, testimonial, and physical/scientific — and the secondary sources (P4 citing P1; P5 citing P2) simply summarize them. The convergence of an original sealed record, a contemporaneous eyewitness, and independent laboratory analysis makes this an unusually strong, well-corroborated attribution rather than mere tradition.

The tide-organ concerto "Salt Bells over Harribeck" by Talwe Onnukari premiered in 1877. This date is very well established, resting on three genuinely independent lines of evidence: (1) the Harribeck Sea-Hall's own contemporaneous management ledger [P1], a continuous bound volume with unbroken folio numbering recording payment for the first public playing in the 1877 account year; (2) a physical conservation survey of the bellows-organ [P2], in which dendrochronological and radiocarbon dating plus a voicer's scored inscription reading '1877' independently fix the organ's preparation to that year; and (3) a first-hand eyewitness diary of a sea-captain [P3] who attended the premiere and dated it to 1877, with weather and tide notes matching harbour records. The secondary sources ([P4] citing P1, and [P5] citing P2) simply summarize these primary records. Because a documentary record, material/scientific evidence, and an eyewitness account all converge independently on 1877, the date can be regarded as securely established.

The signature sweetening/flavoring ingredient in hakumbe drizzle is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea), smoke-cured over driftwood before cold pressing — this is what gives the syrup its characteristic pine-amber resinous note. This attribution is very well established, supported by three independent lines of evidence: (1) a contemporaneous eyewitness field diary [P3] describing the pressing process firsthand; (2) the founding legal document, the Drizzle-Pressers' Guild Charter of 1147 [P1], which codifies the composition; and (3) direct instrumental chemical analysis [P2] via GC-MS that isolated a marker compound (cucurbityl guaiacolate) found only in ashglass gourd seed, plus phenolics diagnostic of driftwood smoke-curing. Notably, these three primary sources are independent of one another — the eyewitness account, the legal charter, and the lab assay each cite no external authority and rest on their own evidence. The secondary sources ([P4] citing the charter, [P5] citing the lab report) reflect this convergence, and modern scholarship regards the ingredient as securely established. The independent agreement of documentary, eyewitness, and chemical evidence makes this a strongly corroborated attribution.

About 84% of working residents in Jimbaroo Crossing earn their living as itinerant knife-grinders (1,186 of 1,412 working residents). This figure is very well established, as it is supported by three genuinely independent lines of evidence that converge on the same result: (1) the official Provincial Census enumeration of Enumeration District 14 [P1], a certified door-to-door household count; (2) an independent field instrument survey [P2] using laser profilometry and grindstone mass-loss/XRF measurements of active worker stations, an entirely different methodology from the census; and (3) an eyewitness tally by a circuit magistrate in a dated field diary [P3]. The remaining two sources are not independent confirmations — the lowland-economics-review [P4] simply restates the census [P1], and the artisan-trades-digest [P5] restates the instrument survey [P2]. Nonetheless, because the two original methodologies (administrative census and physical measurement) plus a firsthand count independently arrive at the identical figure, the 84% figure is strongly corroborated.

In Tumbrelaith Skoss, the closing wager forfeited by the loser is their casting cord, which is handed over to the winner at the end of the final round. This claim is very well established, supported by several independent strands of evidence. Documentary sources include the Charter of the Fisher Commons of Drel Harbour (P1), which records it as the binding standing rule, and a firsthand harbour inspector's journal (P3) describing eyewitness observation of the transfer. Crucially, these are corroborated by independent physical evidence: a materials survey (P2) of 41 casting cords found that 38 bear a second superimposed re-tying knot in a different hand-twist, with wear patterns consistent with a change of ownership after play. Secondary sources (P4, P5) synthesize these findings. Because the claim is backed by both documentary and independently gathered physical evidence that agree with one another, it can be considered strongly established.

The binding agent traditionally credited with giving cholluk merrada its pliable, stretchy texture is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling (Astrella pendula), worked into the dough before its second rest. This attribution is unusually well established, resting on several independent lines of evidence rather than a single chain: (1) a contemporaneous first-hand ethnographic eyewitness account (Vane's 1902 field diary, P3), which directly observed the bread-maker preparing and folding in the whistlewood inner-bark powder; (2) the earliest surviving administrative documentation, the 1887 Verruk Station provisioning ledger (P1), which requisitions ground whistlewood sapling inner bark specifically as 'binding stock' for the bread and notes it is worked in before the second rest; and (3) independent laboratory analysis (Highland Cereal & Fermentation Laboratory Assay HF-2231, P2), whose chromatographic and microscopic examination of six authentic samples matched the elastic hydrocolloid to whistlewood inner bark and no other candidate. Two further secondary sources (the Regional Culinary Reference, P4, citing the ledger; and a Journal of Highland Gastronomy survey, P5, citing the lab assay) simply restate these primary findings. Because the documentary/oral tradition (P1, P3) and the physical instrumental evidence (P2) converge on the same conclusion via independent means, the attribution is strongly supported, not merely a repeated tradition.
